Dear Secretary Reese: 
The Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”), through this filing,1 
submits proposed revisions to its Open Access Transmission, Energy and Operating Reserve 
Markets Tariff (“Tariff”),2 to establish a Large Load Addition Resource Study (“LARS”) process,3 
associated application and operational requirements to enable load and generation to be studied 
together leveraging existing MISO processes to facilitate the timely availability of the tool to 
customers.4  The LARS proposal will help streamline the MISO generator and load interconnection 
process by providing expedited review of the addition of 200 MW or greater loads together with 
new generation resources that are electrically proximate to those loads.  Through this coordinated 
study framework, LARS is designed to facilitate the timely and reliable interconnection of Large 
Loads and new generation onto the MISO system.

threshold for entry into LARS, not all “Large Loads” will be eligible to be a “LARS Associated Load.”

MISO requests that the Tariff revisions submitted herewith be made effective December 2, 
2026, which is not less than sixty (60) days nor more than one-hundred and twenty (120) days 
from the date of this filing.  MISO requests that the Commission issue an order by this date in 
order to allow MISO to commence the first LARS Study Period in Q1 of 2027.  As discussed 
below and in the supporting testimony of Christina Drake,5 action is needed in the near term to 
enhance the available tools to address the reliability impacts associated with the impending 
interconnection of Load, including the anticipated interconnection of significant large loads. 
 
I. 
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 
 
LARS responds to rapidly evolving reliability and resource adequacy needs in the MISO 
region.  MISO is proposing LARS to facilitate the cost effective, timely and reliable integration of 
new large loads into the system.  LARS supports the Commission’s call to action to meet these 
new challenges in short order.  LARS will provide a path for the interconnection of both large 
loads and supporting generation pairs in a parallel 120-day study process.  The proposal leverages 
the existing success in the MISO’s Expedited Project Review (“EPR”) process on the load side 
and lessons learned from Expedited Resource Additions Study (“ERAS”) process on the 
generation side.  
 
MISO is experiencing significant growth in electricity demand at the same time that 
additional resources are needed to reliably serve that demand.  MISO projects annual load growth 
of approximately 1% to 3% through 2044, driven in part by energy-intensive loads such as data 
centers and manufacturing expansion, and has identified the need to accelerate new resource 
additions as demand grows.6   
 
The need to accelerate the infrastructure necessary to reliably serve growing electricity 
demand is also reflected in the Department of Energy’s (“DOE”) Speed to Power initiative, which 
seeks to accelerate development timelines for large-scale transmission and generation projects to 
meet rising electricity demand.7  LARS advances that objective within the MISO region by 
providing a process through which significant new large loads and generation intended to support 
that load can be studied on an accelerated and coordinated basis.

LARS is also responsive to the Commission’s June 18, 2026, Order Instituting Proceeding 
Under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act in Docket No. EL26-70-000 (“Show Cause Order”).  
The Commission preliminarily found, among other things, that MISO’s existing Tariff may be 
unjust and unreasonable because it does not provide generator interconnection study procedures 
and services that account for the operational dynamics of serving electrically proximate large 
loads.8  The Commission specifically addressed the potential for a new generating facility and an 
electrically proximate large load to be studied in a manner that accounts for their combined 
transmission system impacts.9  LARS provides a mechanism for MISO to study a large load and 
the generation that will serve it at the same time such that their combined transmission system 
impacts may be considered together.  
 
In addition, the Commission requested a detailed informational report on any proposals 
under consideration to address the issue of resource adequacy to serve new large loads, strongly 
encouraging new proposals to the extent necessary to address these concerns.10  The LARS process 
responds to this concern and serves to provide a critical tool that allows the timely integration of 
resources associated with these new loads supporting regional resource adequacy.  While MISO’s 
existing processes have been sufficient to ensure resource adequacy in the short term, the unique 
commercial and operational characteristics of new large loads and the speed with which they need 
to come online have prompted MISO to develop LARS as an additional tool to further support 
resource adequacy as new large loads are integrated into the MISO region in the future. 
 
This proposal is deliberately tailored to significant new large loads.  MISO initially 
proposed a minimum eligibility threshold of 250 MW and expressly sought stakeholder input 
regarding whether that threshold appropriately captured high-impact loads without unnecessarily 
expanding the scope of the process.11  MISO set the initial threshold at 250 MW as recent EPR 
results showed that large loads of 250 MW and greater created meaningful grid impacts, with 
upgrades becoming increasingly likely between 300–500 MW and consistently necessary at 1,200 
MW and above with multi-element upgrades.  Stakeholders proposed alternative thresholds, 
including 200 MW, which MISO proposes herein as it expands the LARS proposal beyond 
hyperscale load to apply to other kinds of large loads including industrial loads.12

Importantly, LARS is designed to work in concert with other MISO large load initiatives, 
such as MISO’s proposed Zero Injection Generator Interconnection Agreement (“ZGIA”)13 and 
Interconnection Reliability Requirement (“IRR”)14 frameworks currently pending before the 
Commission and maintains protections for generation already progressing through MISO’s 
generator interconnection queue or more commonly known as the Definitive Planning Phase 
(“DPP”) process.  LARS provides a different tool for large load interconnection arrangements 
involving paired generation that do not fit within the ZGIA framework. 
 
Taken LARS provides MISO with a targeted tool to address the intersection of significant 
large load additions, optimized Network Upgrades with generation and load, generation 
development, and supports resource adequacy.  The proposal allows MISO to study qualifying 
load and associated generation on a coordinated basis, responds to issues identified in the 
Commission’s Show Cause Order, and is designed to preserve the integrity of MISO’s existing 
generator interconnection processes.  LARS is needed now to facilitate the cost-effective and 
reliable interconnection of impending new large loads and generation additions on an accelerated 
timeline. 
 
II. 
OVERVIEW OF THE LARS PROCESS 
 
A. 
BACKGROUND 
 
The MISO region is experiencing a significant change in both the magnitude and pace of 
anticipated electricity demand.  MISO’s 2026 Reliability Imperative explains that, following a 
period in which electricity demand grew at an average annual rate of approximately 0.5% between 
2009 and 2024, MISO now projects annual load growth of approximately 1% to 3% through 
2044.15  MISO identifies energy-intensive loads, including data centers and manufacturing 
expansion, among the sources of this sustained and concentrated growth.16 
 
This growth has corresponding implications for the resources necessary to maintain 
operational reliability and resource adequacy.  MISO has stated that, as demand grows rapidly, 
maintaining existing resources and accelerating new resource additions are critical.17  MISO’s 
2026 Planning Resource Auction results likewise recognize that, although the region has sufficient 
resources to satisfy resource adequacy requirements for the 2026-2027 Planning Year, faster

resource additions remain necessary to support large-load growth and ensure resource adequacy.18  
MISO has, therefore, identified rapid load growth as a core component of its broader Reliability 
Imperative.  MISO’s Transmission Evolution work specifically identifies the need to “speed up 
timelines for new generation and transmission projects” while managing large-load growth without 
compromising reliability.19   
 
Against this backdrop, the challenge presented by new large load growth is not limited to 
connecting the load itself.  Significant new demand must be accompanied by sufficient resources 
to maintain reliability and resource adequacy.  MISO’s Large Load Working Group (“LLWG”) 
was established to address this broader relationship, with a mission encompassing markets, reliable 
operations, planning, and resource adequacy associated with the integration and enablement of 
large loads.20  LARS is intended to address one aspect of that challenge by establishing a process 
through which qualifying Large Load additions and associated new generation can be studied on 
a coordinated basis.  Studying qualifying load and generation together, with aligned study timeline, 
provides a mechanism for MISO to consider significant new demand and the resources associated 
resulting in optimized network upgrades.  In this manner, LARS is designed to facilitate the reliable 
integration of significant new load and generation on an accelerated timeline. 
 
B. 
STRUCTURE OF LARS AND PARTIES 
 
LARS provides a parallel study process for a proposed large load and generation pair.21  As 
MISO explained in its motion for abeyance, “LARS will assess the transmission infrastructure 
needed to meet new large loads and new generation in an efficient process that can be executed on 
a shorter timeline, further supplementing the opportunities available for members to facilitate new 
large spot loads effectively.”22  The generation and load studies will be completed at the same time 
and will finish within approximately 120 days.  To allow this to happen, LARS brings the 
requirements that are needed for both the generation and load studies under a common application,

the LARS Application and provides a framework for participation by the entities involved in the 
existing MISO processes that LARS builds upon.  
 
There are four primary types of entities involved in implementing LARS aside from MISO. 
These are the LARS Associated Transmission Customer, the Interconnection Customer(s) who will 
own or operate the Generating Facility, the applicable Transmission Owner, and the 
owner/controller of the ultimate load (called the “LARS Associated Load”).  To understand how 
LARS will work, a brief explanation of each of these parties’ roles in the process is provided below.   
 
The first of these parties is the LARS Associated Transmission Customer.23  This is the 
entity that procures Transmission Service for load and has a direct relationship with the load.  This 
is often a Load Serving Entity (“LSE”).  Because only the Transmission Customer can procure 
Transmission Service under established Tariff processes, LARS requires the LARS Associated 
Transmission Customer to be the party that initiates the LARS Application and obtains the 
resulting Transmission Service.24  Ultimately, the LARS Associated Transmission Customer acts 
as a coordinator between the other entities involved in the LARS process.  
 
Second, there is the Interconnection Customer.  This is the entity that will complete the 
section of the LARS Application that supports the generation portion of the LARS study, will be 
responsible for meeting the requirements of Attachment X pertaining to the generation study, and 
will receive Interconnection Service under an LLGIA.  The Interconnection Customer can be any 
entity (including an Independent Power Producer (“IPP”)) whose Generating Facility will provide 
Energy for the LARS Associated Load provided it is permitted by applicable laws and regulations 
to do so.25  The Interconnection Customer has the contractual relationships required by LARS to 
show that the Generating Facility is in fact paired with the LARS Associated Load.26   
 
Third, the Transmission Owner owns the facilities the LARS Associated Load will connect 
to the Transmission System.  The Transmission Owner works with the other parties to establish 
the Point of Interconnection (“POI”) for the Generating Facility(ies) and the Point of Withdrawal

The fourth key participant is the entity that owns or controls the LARS Associated Load, 
which for purpose of LARS must be a large load of at least 200 MW.28  While MISO usually will 
not have a direct relationship with this entity and does not purport through this filing to impose 
obligations directly on them, this entity will have a crucial role in establishing relationships 
between the parties directly involved in LARS, in supplying information necessary to complete 
the LARS Application, and study process, and in enabling the other parties to meet their obligations 
under LARS.   
 
As noted above, the roles of these parties and their specific responsibilities reflect existing 
Tariff requirements and practices.  LARS does not seek to fundamentally change the established 
roles of the entities participating in the load and generation studies but rather seeks to coordinate 
them.  LARS thus provides for faster and more transparent interconnection arrangements for large 
loads with paired generation, while offering customers speed-to-power, optimized transmission 
solutions, and greater certainty to support siting, and financing of large load projects.  The outcome 
of the LARS process is MTEP approval of transmission required to reliably facilitate the 
withdrawal of the load and corresponding injection rights for the proposed generation. The 
component parts of the process are discussed in greater detail below.  
 
C. 
THE LARS APPLICATION 
MISO is establishing a single application process for the participants in the LARS process.  
The LARS Application will be a single submission consisting of materials required by Attachment 
FF for the load and Attachment X for the generation.29  Because LARS involves two separate study 
processes being completed concurrently and in parallel, all the relevant parties to the load and 
generation pairing must apply together.30  While the LARS Application process may only be 
initiated by the LARS Associated Transmission Customer, the Interconnection Customer, the 
Transmission Owner, and the LARS Associated Load customer must all complete the required 
information as part of the application before it will be reviewed by MISO.  Independent Power 
Producers and other kinds of Interconnection Customers are not prohibited from participating in

required by the load and generation study processes.  A non-refundable fee of $250,000 must

Notably, MISO is establishing a “pre-submission coordination process” that LARS 
applicants must participate in prior to submitting a LARS Application.33  This coordination process 
requires the potential LARS Interconnection Customer and the Transmission Owner to meet and 
agree on a definitive Point of Interconnection for the proposed LARS Generating Facility.  Forty-
five days prior to a LARS Application deadline, a potential LARS Interconnection Customer must 
notify the Transmission Owner to whose Transmission Facilities the potential LARS 
Interconnection Customer proposes to Interconnect of its plans to participate in LARS.  After 
receiving a request to meet from any potential LARS Interconnection Customer, the Transmission 
Owner must meet with them and any other impacted parties necessary to determine a definitive 
POI within ten business days after receiving a request for the meeting.  The parties must jointly 
agree on a feasible POI no later than ten business days prior to the next LARS Application deadline 
as published on MISO’s website.  An attestation from the Transmission Owner stating that it has 
an agreed POI with the LARS Interconnection Customer(s) must be included in the LARS 
Application.34  
 
MISO is proposing these pre-submission coordination activities for several reasons.  First, 
while the LARS Associated Transmission Customer is the only party that may submit the LARS 
Application, MISO is requiring that they actively participate in the LARS process with the 
potential LARS Interconnection Customers prior to LARS Application deadline.  Second, 
requiring pre-submission coordination activities will increase the efficiency of reviewing the 
LARS Application with all the relevant parties identified, the agreed upon POI identified, and other 
necessary details have already been determined by the time the LARS Application is submitted to 
MISO.  Having the LARS Application parties agree on many of these necessary details in advance 
of submission will also help avoid future disagreements or changes, which can lead to unnecessary 
or late withdrawals from the study process.  MISO has heard from stakeholders and learned from 
experience that an accelerated study process requires that the relevant participants have 
coordinated and agreed upon key details (such as the location of the POI) up front and not after 
they have submitted their application. Third, requiring coordination meetings between these parties 
will assist them with identifying any other relevant parties who may need to participate in the 
LARS process.  Ms. Drake explains that to effectively facilitate the speed of the LARS study 
process, MISO needs all relevant parties to the load and generation pair to not only be identified 
at the outset but committed to working together.35

MISO will accept LARS Applications on a rolling basis, and the applications will be 
queued on a serial, time-stamped basis based on time of submission to the LARS process.  There 
will be three LARS study periods each year and each study period will be completed in 
approximately 120 days, as explained by Ms. Drake.36  MISO will accept ten LARS Applications 
per study period and the LARS Applications will be assigned to study periods in order of 
submission.  Customers interested in joining the next LARS study period must submit their LARS 
Application to MISO no later than 20 business days prior to the scheduled kick-off of the LARS 
study period as published on the MISO public website.  MISO will keep an open queue of LARS 
Applications and will replace any LARS Application that withdraw prior to study kick off with the 
next submitted generation/load pair not included in the current study period.  Once the LARS study 
process has kicked off for a specific LARS generation/load pair, then that spot is lost for the LARS 
study period it is part of even if the pair later withdraws during the study process.37   
 
An Interconnection Request included in a LARS Application must be accompanied by an 
executed agreement between the Interconnection Customer and either the LARS Associated 
Tranmission Customer or the entity that owns or controls the LARS Associated Load.  The 
agreement must demonstrate that the output of the LARS Generating Facility will serve the LARS 
Associated Load.  The agreement must be legally binding and must state a minimum term of five 
years so that if any transmission solutions need to be developed, there is sufficient time to work 
through the processes for development.  As described in Section 3.12.2(i) of Attachment X, the 
agreement must be in the form of a power purchase agreement (“PPA”) or similar off-take 
agreement, a Build-Own-Transfer Agreement, or any other kind of agreement used by Load 
Serving Entities including a special contract, a large load tariff agreement, or a retail service 
agreement.  Ms. Drake explains that in response to stakeholder feedback, MISO revised the Tariff 
redlines to explicitly state the agreement can be executed between the generator and large load. 38 
This does not supersede the role of the LARS Associated Transmission Customer to determine 
whether to submit a LARS Application but does allow flexibility for different types of agreements 
that are consistent with state law and supported by the parties.39  MISO also added the third 
agreement option to incorporate specific utility arrangements with large loads that are not 
traditional PPAs to link the generation and load.40

Other requirements of the LARS Application include limiting the Interconnection Requests 
to NRIS, limiting the amount of requested Interconnection Service to no more than 150% of the 
peak demand of the LARS Associated Load, and demonstration of 100% site control for the POI 
including a one-line diagram demonstrating the Generating Facilities and any associated electrical 
equipment required.41  Based on stakeholder feedback MISO established the 150% of 
Interconnection Service limitation to ensure the generation is required to reliably serve the load 
within the same LRZ.  As Ms. Drake states, MISO sought to establish a closer connection between 
what is needed by the LARS Associated Load and what is being proposed by the LARS 
Interconnection Customer.42  Thus, MISO implemented this requirement to directly connect the 
Generating Facility with the LARS Associated Load and to allow for different generator fuel types 
and accreditation.  Ms. Drake explains that “this requirement establishes a clear connection 
between the output of the Generating Facility and the load without being overly prescriptive on 
generation fuel type, dispatch requirements, or other operational considerations.”43 
 
Another important condition of the LARS process is the requirement that the load and 
generation pair be located in the same Local Resource Zone (“LRZ”).44  The Point of 
Interconnection(s) specified in a LARS Application must be located in the same LRZ as the Point 
of Withdrawal (“POW”) of the LARS Associated Load.  As discussed by Ms. Drake, the intent of 
the LARS process is to identify an optimized Network Upgrade solution for both the load and 
generation, and MISO retains that flexibility in the LRZ because it aligns with MISO’s Resource 
Adequacy construct.45  Specifically, MISO does not have a requirement that loads bring generation, 
but through the proposed LARS process, by restricting the Point of Interconnection(s) specified in 
a LARS Application to be located in the same LRZ as the Point of Withdrawal, MISO providing 
an incentive for Load to bring Generation in a manner that maximizes the positive impact this 
Generation has on Resource Adequacy.  MISO recognizes there are other ways it could have 
limited the pairing such as requiring the generation and LARS Associated Load to be located in 
the same Local Balancing Authority area or through requiring that the location of the Generating 
Facilities be within a specific number of substations of the LARS Associated Load.  However, 
limiting the pairing of Generating Facilities and LARS Associated Load to the same LRZ strikes 
an appropriate balance between accommodating large, landlocked LARS Associated Loads that 
may need additional POIs to propose sufficient Generating Facilities needed to serve that load.

MISO is proposing to increase flexibility in the LARS process by allowing a LARS 
Associated Load to be served by multiple Generating Facilities under specific circumstances.  
First, all Generating Facilities serving a LARS Associated Load must be included and identified 
in the same LARS Application and must request a minimum of 200 MW of Generator 
Interconnection Service in aggregate.  Second, a LARS Associated Load may be served by more 
than one group of Generating Facilities located at different POIs, but a separate LARS Application 
must be submitted for each POI group of Generating Facilities.  Stated differently, each group of 
aggregated LARS Generating Facilities at a single POI must submit a separate LARS Application.  
Each LARS Application must identify the total amount of load requested by the LARS Associated 
Load and must identify every Generating Facility providing power to that load.46  While MISO is 
allowing aggregation for LARS Generating Facilities, MISO is not allowing aggregated load to 
participate in LARS.  As explained earlier, MISO developed LARS in the context of dramatic large
